title: 7 CRASHED Stocks to BUY for EPIC UPSIDE‼️

steps.does: Opens the video by stating the public account's total value (new all-time high, about $5.288 million) and the day's dollar gain (about $67,000).
steps.why: Frames the market backdrop as party time before moving to the stock-picking exercise.
steps.conclusion: Portfolio is at an all-time high; enjoy it because a 6-18 month bear market will eventually come.

steps.does: Shows the AMD position page from a brokerage app screenshot: total value, shares, average cost, total and today's gain/loss, then the purchase-history lots table (acquired date, quantity, average cost, gain/loss per lot). Also mentions Meta's day gain and a Halloween 2022 lot.
steps.why: To show how a single winner has grown to dominate the portfolio and how a small percentage move now moves dollars a lot.
data: Meta lot bought Halloween 2022 up $444K on a $60K buy
steps.conclusion: Position size is now so big that a 2% move is a $37K swing.

steps.does: For each of seven picks (Wynn, Netflix, SoFi, RH, McDonald's, Celsius and one more) shows a brokerage-app price chart screenshot with the past-year percent change and hand-writes the rank number (e.g. #1 of 7, #6 of 7) on it.
steps.why: Criterion for the exercise is that every pick must be a crashed stock, not one at or near all-time highs.
data: McDonald's down over 30% from highs 5-6 months ago
steps.conclusion: Each qualifies as a crash stock with a multi-year (3-5 year) upside thesis.

steps.does: For Wynn, reads trailing-12-month adjusted EBITDA by property (Las Vegas $890M, Peninsula $386M, Wynn Palace $769M, Boston $222M) and a graphic of each property's share of EBITDA, and compares the new Middle East property with Marina Bay Sands ($3B EBITDA best case, $300-500M conservative estimates).
steps.why: For resort companies depreciation is huge and non-cash, so EBITDA gives a truer view of property earnings than net income or EPS.
steps.conclusion: Properties are EBITDA machines, so the 38% drop is a buying opportunity to build a good-sized position over the next few months.

steps.does: Says Netflix trades at a forward P/E of roughly 20 despite recurring subscriptions, pricing power, international growth and an ads business; for SoFi and RH discusses growth potential and leverage risk qualitatively.
steps.why: Argues the market is pricing multi-lever growth companies too cheaply.
steps.conclusion: Netflix is an easy buy at that multiple; RH and SoFi are good opportunities if leverage is kept in check.

rules.text: Only pick stocks that have actually crashed, not ones at or near all-time highs.
For resort and property companies use adjusted EBITDA instead of net income or EPS because depreciation is large and non-cash.

steps.does: Plays a CNBC Television YouTube clip of Fundstrat's Tom Lee ('Next six months will be most important for inflation'), with a markets ticker (Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq, Russell 2000) on screen, pausing to comment; disagrees with Lee at 30:11 on the importance of memory-chip costs.
steps.why: To gather an analyst's view on yields, inflation, Fed policy and the market, then give a counterview.
data: Dow 51,330, S&P 500 7,706, Nasdaq 26,937, Russell 2000 2,832 on the ticker
steps.conclusion: Says he fundamentally disagrees with Lee: memory affects almost everything electronic and big tech is raising ad prices to fund chip spending.
